newsitem.title: UK: Discontent prompts SIB to urge LME board changes.
newsitem.headline: Discontent prompts SIB to urge LME board changes.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) users told the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) they were unhappy with the board structure, prompting the regulator to call for a shake-up.
The SIB said in its wide-ranging review of the exchange that the board should be re-organised to avoid potential conflict of interest and better represent the membership.

"The present arrangements are regarded by many as favouring the ring members unduly. As a result the board is widely regarded as being out of touch with the LME's broader membership," the report, published on Thursday, said.
Ring members account for half the LME board's total membership of 16.
"A substantial number of those consulted attached considerable importance to the need for more directors having no current association with the metal industry," it added.
Representatives of trading firms sit on the board, making decisions on commercial as well as regulatory matters.
"People may be reluctant to provide information if they think it is not secure," David Pritchard, the SIB official who lead the review team, told Reuters.

Regulatory decisions must not be seen to be influenced by board members' own commercial, sectional or personal interests, the report added. Regulatory functions should be transferred to a strengthened executive or to an independent committee.
The full board now sets trading and contract rules.
"We recommend the establishment of a market conduct committee to oversee both the setting and routine enforcement of such rules and regulations on behalf of the board," the report said.
The LME executive needs more staffing and resources since its staff has only doubled to 44 since 1987, despite a seven-fold increase in business and three times more members, the SIB report said.
Only 17 staff members work wholly or partly in regulation.
"The regulatory and enforcement functions need a sharper focus and higher profile at a senior level through the creation of the post of head of market regulation and enforcement," the report said.
"Unless this is done, there will be continuing difficulty in achieving the successful delegation of market surveillance and enforcement responsibilities to the executive," it added.
